items.title: @rasbt：Catching up on the 10 (!) open LLM architecture releases from the past month. Quite a lot happened in October. I guess w
items.abstract_or_text: Catching up on the 10 (!) open LLM architecture releases from the past month. Quite a lot happened in October. I guess we can call it "Open October"! 1. Kolibri-1 (78B): A notable model from Germany. Features classic Grouped Query Attention (GQA) and Sliding Window Attention (SWA) attention module. 2. Ling 3.1 Flash (560B): Uses Kimi Delta Attention and the eighth uses gated Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) inspired by DeepSeek. 3. Muse Spark Open (816B): Besides Musse Glimmer, the first major open weight release from Meta (since Llama). Uses classic GQA + SWA but adds a LatentMoE. 4. Nemotron 3.5 Super VL (120B): Combines Mamba-2 layers with just eight attention layers. Also LatentMoE 5. Dory1.0 (4B): A looped transformer design. 6. Reflection Beam (501B): GQA+SWA architecture. 7. Recursive Flint (40B): Note that "Recursive" is the company name; the architecture is a fairly standard MoE with GQA and SWA. 8. MiniMax M3.1-Flash (428B): Uses their own MiniMax Sparse Attention module. 9. LFM3 (1.7B): Hybrid architecture that mixes short convolutions and attention. 10. Mistral Large 4 (1T) combines MLA with sparse attention. Will probably cover/discuss things in more depth in the coming weeks!

items.title: @AnthropicAI：New Anthropic research: progress on provable inference for large language models. Here, we introduce FlashProve. Buildin
items.abstract_or_text: New Anthropic research: progress on provable inference for large language models. Here, we introduce FlashProve. Building on established cryptographic techniques, FlashProve allows developers to verify whether a given response came from a given AI model. It’s substantially more efficient than prior open-source methods for doing so. These proofs have a range of applications. They can, for instance, make it harder for attackers to hijack a chat, or enable safety evaluators to verify that the model they’re testing is the same one being served to customers. Further progress in provable inference will likely be an important part of improving trust in AI deployment. To that end, we're open-sourcing FlashProve’s code.

items.title: @random_walker：As AI labs race toward Recursive Self Improvement, there’s a possibility that what they are actually racing toward is Re
items.abstract_or_text: As AI labs race toward Recursive Self Improvement, there’s a possibility that what they are actually racing toward is Recursive Self Extinction — of their business model. Here’s my reasoning. 1. Progress on verifiable tasks continues. In particular, improving the cost efficiency of existing capabilities is a highly verifiable task. For the past few years, cost per equivalent capability has dropped by at least 10x per year. 2. Progress on most unverifiable tasks remains frustratingly hard. AI inherits the same limitations (ambiguous success criteria, slow and noisy feedback) that limit human performance at tasks ranging from writing to governance. 3. RSI ends up being narrow. Even if some version of RSI is achieved, it results in an explosion in some dimensions (efficiency, verifiable tasks) while falling short of producing something that is superintelligent in any real sense. 4. More than one lab stays at the frontier. This means the market will remain competitive, and developers can’t charge high margins to compensate for rapidly falling inference prices. 5. Jevons’ paradox is not a magic bullet. There are very few applications that will consume so many tokens that they could generate the astronomical amounts of revenue implied by the labs’ valuations. 6. What about scientific research? Even if it’s true that AI could enable great scientific innovations, I don’t think AI companies will make much money off of that. 7. The one escape hatch is moving “up the stack”, transitioning from selling tokens to an enterprise software like model that relies on high switching costs.

items.abstract_or_text: Over the past year, we've built platforms, trained foundation models, worked with biotech companies, achieved wet-lab validation, broken things, and iterated again and again. One belief kept getting stronger: the future of drug discovery isn't isolated AI predictions. It's continuous engineering and optimization driven by experimental evidence. I believe the next breakthroughs will come from small teams of 5–10 scientists. There are too many diseases to tackle, targets to discover, and molecules to engineer and advance into the clinic. Today, LiteFold is generally available to help make that possible. Own your research. Control your data. Use the best models. Learn from experiments. Keep improving. Hill Climb Biology.

items.title: @GiacomoFenzi：I am happy to share FlashProve: our performant open-source prototype for provable inference. We believe that this has si
items.abstract_or_text: I am happy to share FlashProve: our performant open-source prototype for provable inference. We believe that this has significant implications for security, pacing AI development, integrity guarantees, and more. FlashProve allows a provider to commit to model weights, and then prove that replies originate from the committed model. The proof leaks no information about the weights, and the verifier can efficiently verify it on consumer hardware. Our library is performant, proving a 400B parameter MoE model at 100 tok/s. We have open-sourced the associated code and Lean formalization. We hope that it catalyzes further progress in verification of inference, and look forward to seeing it.

items.title: @MSFTResearch：What if knowing the rules isn't the same as knowing what to do? For Mike Walker, who leads projects at the intersection
items.abstract_or_text: What if knowing the rules isn't the same as knowing what to do? For Mike Walker, who leads projects at the intersection of AI, cybersecurity, and large distributed systems at Microsoft Research, understanding a system starts with understanding its rules—but expertise also requires something more nuanced: knowing how those rules operate in context. In a new Microsoft Research Podcast episode, Walker joins Principal Technical Program Manager Weishung Liu to talk cybersecurity, hacker culture, autonomous systems, leadership, and what his personal and professional challenges have taught him about judgment and adaptability.
